record.paper_title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning
record.original_question: For practical federated-learning systems, how can composite objective functions and automatic tuning algorithms balance model quality, convergence speed, throughput, fairness, privacy, robustness, and server or client resource use when these goals conflict?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a federated learning system in which a central server coordinates training of a shared model with a population of clients. The performance of such a system is described by a vector of metrics

  M = (q, c, t, f, p, r, u_s, u_c),

where q denotes model quality (e.g., test accuracy or loss on a held-out distribution), c denotes convergence speed (e.g., number of communication rounds to reach a target loss), t denotes training throughput (e.g., examples processed per unit time across the federation), f denotes a fairness measure (e.g., variance or worst-case loss across clients), p denotes a privacy guarantee (e.g., the (ε, δ) parameters of differential privacy or another quantitative leakage bound), r denotes a robustness measure (e.g., accuracy under a specified family of adversarial or Byzantine perturbations), u_s denotes server-side resource usage, and u_c denotes client-side resource usage (compute, memory, energy, bandwidth).

The system is governed by a vector θ ∈ Θ of tunable parameters (such as client learning rate, server learning rate, batch size, number of local steps, number of clients sampled per round, compression level, clipping threshold, noise multiplier, aggregation weights, and similar quantities). Each evaluation M(θ) is expensive, noisy, and often only partially observable, and the components of M are typically in conflict.

Formulate and analyze:

(a) A principled methodology for defining a composite scalar objective J(M) (or, equivalently, a Pareto-based criterion) that faithfully reflects practitioner preferences over the eight components of M while remaining well-posed under noise and partial observability;

(b) An automatic tuning algorithm A: histories of (θ_i, M̂(θ_i)) → θ_{next} that, with high probability and using a budget polynomial in |Θ| and the noise level, returns parameters θ* whose attained metric vector is approximately Pareto-optimal (or near-optimal for J) among all feasible θ ∈ Θ subject to user-specified hard constraints on any subset of {q, c, t, f, p, r, u_s, u_c};

(c) Provable trade-off guarantees quantifying how improvements in any one component of M must degrade at least one other component, in a federated setting where data heterogeneity, client availability, and privacy/robustness constraints are explicitly modeled.

Provide such a composite objective, such a tuning algorithm, and such trade-off guarantees, or prove obstructions showing that no algorithm meeting these requirements can exist within stated computational or statistical budgets.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent surveys and papers on multi-objective federated learning and federated hyperparameter tuning (2021–2025) treat composite-objective design and automatic tuning balancing accuracy, fairness, privacy, robustness, and resource use as an active, unresolved research area. Partial methods exist (FedEx, FLoRA, FMOL, multi-objective NAS for FL), but no general algorithm with provable trade-off guarantees across all listed objectives is established.

status_evidence.title: Multi-objective methods in Federated Learning: A survey and taxonomy
status_evidence.snippet: Current work can be divided into multi-objective neural architecture search and more general multi-objective hyperparameter tuning... remains active area.
status_evidence.claim: Multi-objective FL tuning is an open, active research area as of 2025.

status_evidence.title: Federated Hyperparameter Tuning: Challenges, Baselines, and Connections to Weight-Sharing
status_evidence.snippet: Different federated learning applications have diverse training preferences... selecting optimal hyperparameters is burdensome.
status_evidence.claim: Automatic FL hyperparameter tuning balancing competing objectives remains a recognized open challenge.

status_evidence.title: Federated Multi-Objective Learning (OpenReview)
status_evidence.snippet: FMOL framework allows multiple clients to distributively solve a multi-objective optimization problem.
status_evidence.claim: Only partial frameworks exist; no comprehensive solution covering all eight metrics with provable guarantees.
